posts.title: pushin P(aper)
posts.subtitle: Oranges in the Shower
paragraphs: Porch, marker, blank worksheet. I'd been designing this thing for weeks and finally got a printer to bridge the digital and physical worlds.

This was meant to help me document audio projects. Field notes for a discipline that doesn't really have field notes. And after playing with a few different formats I figured I’d fill one out to test it.
I don’t know where it came from. But by the time I’d finished doodling the raindrops around the title, the page already had ingredients:
rain recording from Tettegouche
spaced-out electric ukulele
maybe something funky on the synth: pads, arp, brass + auto filter
bass guitar FUNK
This project I hadn’t made a thing for already had more of an identity than stuff that’s been on my hard drive for years.
Writing a title and fleshing out a sonic idea before touching an instrument. Something about that felt like a breakthrough.
I have spent absurd amounts of time trying to solve creative organization through software:
Naming conventions for audio files.
Folder hierarchies on hard drives.
Tagging systems.
Color-coded session templates.
Automations that would generate timestamps and project IDs and dump everything into the right place.
Each one started clean.
Each one collapsed within weeks into a graveyard of “Untitled_47” and “MIX_FINAL_v3_actually_final.”

The problem was never the software. It was that I was trying to organize work that didn't have a center yet. Software organizes what already exists. The structure I needed was the kind that exists before the work does.
Writing the title with a marker forced a center. You can’t write Oranges in the Shower on a piece of paper and then make a generic four-on-the-floor track.
The phrase is now a friendly mission.
Whatever I make has to reach for it.
Oranges in the Shower might become an album. It might become my new personal shower soundtrack that I never post on Spotify. It might become a substack post (cough cough).
The point is not whether the project evolves into a masterpiece. It’s that a unit of intention now exists in real life.

It’s attached to a moment on a specific day, in my own handwriting, on paper that won’t have an automatic update or run out of cloud storage, but could very well end up with smudges, stains, and water damage (YES!!!).
This is a core aspect to soundbending, at least as I understand it (been meaning to schedule a call with Rick Rubin, tbd)…
A willingness to commit to something specific enough to recognize and exciting enough to chase, then letting that constraint pull you toward a finished idea.
and then letting that constraint pull you towards a finished idea.
For me, every worksheet is a small, complete, repeatable piece. Each one stands alone. Each one stacks with the others.
Lego pieces. Substack posts. Archive. Portfolio.
Some will become music. Some will become writing. Some will sit unfinished forever and that’s cool too.
Here’s what oranges in the shower sounded like to me in April 2026:
Kidding! But not really…
More like: Here's what I chose to represent the idea of oranges in the shower, using a sample I have that means something to me.
I had surprise plans after the porch that day and since I wasn’t able to “record a song”, it’s been on my to-do list for weeks and today was my deadline.
Who says I need to record an original track for this?
Who says it can’t be a voicememo??
Who says it’s any less meaningful either way?
Hah!!!
Posted!!!
Premeditation, imagination, intention, identity.
Trying to develop some gravity in one spot within the attention blackhole that is modern society.

posts.title: 32 in Minneapolis | 83 in Dakar
posts.subtitle: what i learned from listening to things in faraway places
paragraphs: 32 degrees, cloudy, late March, Monday afternoon in Minneapolis.
I wanted to feel hope, and I didn’t want an algorithm to guess what that meant.
So instead of filtering my library to “Relaxing” or surrendering to some Spotify station, I opened radio.garden and started looking for somewhere warm.
Radio.garden is essentially a 3D map of the earth covered in green dots, each one a city with its top radio stations. You click a dot, you’re there. No queue, no recommendations, no smart shuffle.
Just a place, its frequencies, and a group of strangers listening together, separately.
Dakar had everything I was looking for that Monday.
Songs I’d never heard, in languages I don’t speak, consistently blowing my mind.
My room suddenly warmer. My hips infinitely looser.

If a song grabbed me I’d navigate to that station’s website to try to find it. Leading me to see local news headlines, community programs, dispatches from a city I’ve never visited, and information I likely wouldn’t have ever seen otherwise.
One tab became three. Three became an hour.
This is what convenience has quietly been costing us.

Spotify is a miracle of access. I can have fourteen years of library-building on my phone at 40,000 feet. I can hijack my friend’s Spotify jam while they’re driving. I’m not arguing against unlimited access.
But somewhere in all the frictionless systems we’ve built and pay for monthly, the artist became a byproduct, and the art a commodity.
There are songs I genuinely love in my library where I couldn’t tell you the artist’s name, the origin, or what the project was even about.
For the longest time there was always a receipt.
Even in the era of iTunes you still had to say
“Yes, Mr. Sean. I Am Down. And I am willing to give you $1.29 to listen to Down for the rest of my life.”
The receipt meant something.
Radio.garden gives a different kind of receipt. Not a transaction, but a place, a shared moment — sounds other people were hearing simultaneously on the other side of the planet.
We're deep in an era where the tools promising the least friction are quietly flattening everything else (for only $12.99/month).

I’m not asserting radio is any more of a representative cultural experience than Spotify. But it felt human in a way I hadn’t expected. Less like a library and more like an open window onto a street I’ve never walked down.
I may never get to travel to Senegal, but I do feel enriched having thought about the people listening with me today.
Sometimes the detour is the point. And after years of streaming music, I’m looking for more detours.

posts.title: Sound
posts.subtitle: memories, mediums, musics
paragraphs: I’ve loved music my whole life.

But piano lessons killed it for a while. Sit here. Read this. Play it exactly like this. Music felt like a language I had to master before I was allowed to speak. So somewhere in middle school I stopped creating and just became a listener instead.
Which honestly wasn’t bad.

In high school I had 150 Pandora stations I’d cycle through till 3am looking for new artists, new songs, new genres. I made playlists and hijacked aux cords like my life depended on it. And for years that’s what my relationship with sound looked like. Engaged, passionate, but a lingering sense that I was orbiting something I couldn’t quite touch.

And then I took 7 years to complete my undergrad. Five different majors, two transfers, a pandemic-induced gap year, and a host of identity crises both personally and creatively. As I wrapped up my sociology degree I had just enough room to take an elective of my choosing.
A class called Sound Studies. Dry title, dry class - changed everything. First assignment: go outside and record. No music. No performing. Just documenting.
Nothing about it felt important at the time, which is probably why it worked.

Somewhere in those lessons sound started becoming a medium instead of a destination. Along with that, making a song for SoundCloud started feeling so specific, maybe even insincere. I didn’t know what to call what I was doing anymore.
Producer felt wrong. Composer felt too avant garde. Engineer felt like a specialized degree.
I was doing parts of all of these roles, but none of them felt relatable or encompassing. Nonetheless, I kept recording things, and kept being confused about it.

Listening back months later. Years later. The hum of a dorm I don’t live in anymore. My dad reading my niece a story. A vocal take where the goofing around in the background is more meaningful than the melody.
Why are these voice memos more meaningful to me than the midwest hip-hop banger I spent three months producing?
They weren’t recordings. They were artifacts.
Soundwaves acting as portals.
Pulling me back into rooms I’d long left.
That's not a music thing. That's a human thing.
Sound doesn’t just document. It teleports. You’re not remembering the moment. You’re back inside it.
Most of the time we type instead.

A voicemail lands differently than a text. Timing, tone, breath, hesitation. Embedded humanity that never survives translation. The fact that Teams still doesn’t have a voice note feature isn’t just a product gap. It’s a symptom of how much we’ve neglected the depth of sound.
That’s what I kept circling back to. So I made a word for it.
Not to define anything. More to avoid having to.
No genres. No job titles. Just sound as a medium.
Something you can do without needing to explain what you’re doing first.
This is the diary of that practice.
